### ek.requires_extra(extra, , packages=None)

Decorator: fail with an actionable install hint if an extra is missing.

The wrapped callable runs only once every package in `packages` imports; the
common case (everything installed) adds a single cheap import check.

* **Parameters:**
  * **extra** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The extra name, used in the hint `pip install ek[<extra>]`.
  * **packages** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterable)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]]) – Import names to probe (defaults to `[extra]`).
* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)

### Example

```pycon
>>> @requires_extra("ocr", packages=["definitely_not_installed_pkg"])
... def run():
...     return "ran"
>>> try:
...     run()
... except MissingExtraError as e:
...     print("ek[ocr]" in str(e))
True
```

Resolve a table parser reference (a registered name or a callable) to a callable.

The risk-coverage trade-off: `{threshold, coverage, selective_risk}` per point.

Coverage is the fraction auto-accepted at each threshold; selective risk is the

### ek.rover(hypotheses, , use_confidence=True, conf_weight=0.5, null_conf=0.7, tokenize=None, max_tokens=5000)

Align N hypotheses, vote per slot, and emit consensus + per-position agreement.

* **Parameters:**
  * **hypotheses** ([`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterable)[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – The recognizer/extractor outputs to fuse. Each may be a string,
    an `OcrResult`-shaped object (`.text`/`.mean_confidence`), a list of
    token strings, or a list of `(token, confidence)` pairs.
  * **use_confidence** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – Blend confidence into the vote (`True`) or vote purely by
    frequency (`False`, which forces `conf_weight` to `0`).
  * **conf_weight** ([`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Weight on average confidence vs vote frequency in the slot score
    (Fiscus’s `1 - alpha`); `0` is frequency-only, `1` is
    confidence-only. Ignored when `use_confidence` is `False`.
  * **null_conf** ([`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Confidence credited to a NULL vote (an engine that produced no
    token at a slot) – the lever for how readily a deletion wins.
  * **tokenize** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`List`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.List)[[`Tuple`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Tuple)[[`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)], [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]]]]) – Optional `hypothesis -> [(token, confidence), ...]` override; by
    default `_as_units()` handles strings/OcrResults/token lists.
  * **max_tokens** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Reject any hypothesis longer than this (the aligner is
    `O(N*l*L*L')`; an unbounded input is a quadratic time/memory DoS).
    `None` disables the guard.
* **Return type:**
  [`RoverConsensus`](_autosummary/ek.qe.html.md#ek.qe.RoverConsensus)
* **Returns:**
  A [`RoverConsensus`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.RoverConsensus) with the consensus `tokens`/`text`, the per-slot
  breakdown, and the per-consensus-token `agreement` usable as a raw signal.

### ek.run_suite(agent, tasks, , k=1, check=None, metrics=None, price=None, prices=None, run=None, seed=None, persist=False, run_id=None, rootdir=None)

Run `agent` over a task suite, `k` trials per task, and report reliability + cost.

* **Parameters:**
  * **agent** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`TaskSpec`](_autosummary/ek.agents.base.html.md#ek.agents.base.TaskSpec)], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – The system under test: `TaskSpec -> Episode` (a bare answer is wrapped). It
    receives the whole spec – `.input`, `.tools`, `.gold` – not just the input.
    If it accepts a keyword `seed`, the per-trial seed is passed to it.
  * **tasks** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – [`TaskSpec`](_autosummary/ek.agents.base.html.md#ek.agents.base.TaskSpec) s (or a `{task_id: spec}` mapping).
  * **k** ([`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Trials per task. `k > 1` is what makes `pass^k` meaningful – and it only means
    anything if the agent is genuinely stochastic (the report warns if it is not).
  * **check** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – The success oracle – a registered checker name or an `(episode, gold) -> bool`
    callable. Defaults to `"output"`; **inject a state-based/executable oracle** for a
    real suite, and run it isolated from the agent.
  * **metrics** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)]) – Optional `{name: Metric}` scored on every episode against `task.gold`, with
    the **suite’s Layer-A grammar injected** – this is how the tool/argument cost
    weights reach a `tool_call`/`trajectory` metric. Results land in
    `report.detail["metrics"]`.
  * **price/prices** – Rates for costing the episodes (see [`ek.agents.cost`](_autosummary/ek.agents.cost.html.md#module-ek.agents.cost)).
  * **run** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`RunProvenance`](_autosummary/ek.agents.base.html.md#ek.agents.base.RunProvenance)]) – [`RunProvenance`](_autosummary/ek.agents.base.html.md#ek.agents.base.RunProvenance) for this run (model, simulator, suite
    version, scaffold). Recorded on every episode and on any baseline saved from it.
  * **seed** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)]) – Base RNG seed. Trial *i* of each task uses `seed + i`: it is recorded on the
    episode’s provenance **and passed to the agent** when the agent accepts a `seed`
    keyword.
  * **persist/run_id/rootdir** – Persist the run to the `runs`/`results` stores.
* **Return type:**
  [`ReliabilityReport`](_autosummary/ek.agents.html.md#ek.agents.ReliabilityReport)
* **Returns:**
  A [`ReliabilityReport`](_autosummary/ek.agents.html.md#ek.agents.ReliabilityReport) carrying `pass@k`, `pass^k` (with
  a bootstrap CI), the success rate (with a Wilson CI), the per-slice cuts, and the cost
  report – because reliability without cost is only half the answer.

### ek.schema_validator(value, , spec=None)

A spec-driven [`Validator`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Validator): type and `domain` checks from a FieldSpec.

Reads the [`FieldSpec`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.FieldSpec) `type` and `domain` – a `(lo, hi)`

### ek.split_conformal_quantile(scores, alpha)

The split-conformal threshold: the `ceil((n+1)(1-alpha)) / n` empirical quantile.

`scores` are nonconformity scores on an exchangeable calibration set. Returns
`+inf` when `n` is too small to guarantee `1 - alpha` (so nothing is
flagged – the honest behaviour at that sample size), and `-inf` at the
`alpha -> 1` limit (flag everything).

### ek.table_from_ocr(ocr_result, , parser=None)

Extract a normalized [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) from an `OcrResult`.

The single seam ek’s table metrics (TEDS / GriTS) use to score OCR table output
uniformly. Returns the recovered Table, or `None` when the result carries no
recoverable table structure.

* **Parameters:**
  * **ocr_result** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Any `OcrResult`-shaped object. ek reads only its `.raw` (the
    engine-specific payload), `.markdown` (VLM/markdown engines), and
    `.meta` – never ocracy types, so any `image -> OcrResult` callable’s
    output works.
  * **parser** ([`Union`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Union)[[`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]]) – 

    How to turn the raw payload into a table (dependency injection /
    open-closed). One of:
    - `None` (default): try the built-in **safe heuristics** – `.raw` is
      already a [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table), a 2-D grid, or a
      `<table>...</table>` HTML string; or `.raw`/`.meta` is a mapping
      carrying one of `{tables, table, cells, grid, html}`; or `.markdown`
      contains an HTML `<table>`. Returns `None` if none match – it never
      guesses wildly.
    - a `str`: the name of a parser registered under `"table_parsers"`
      (per-engine extractor), resolved from [`ek.registry`](_autosummary/ek.registry.html.md#module-ek.registry).
    - a callable `(raw) -> Table | grid | html | None`: an inline per-engine
      extractor. It receives the result’s `.raw` (falling back to the result
      itself when there is no `.raw`).
  * **through** (*Any non-None value an injected parser returns is fed*)
* **Return type:**
  [*Table*](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) | *None*

:param [`Table.coerce()`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.Table.coerce):
:param so a parser may yield a Table:
:param a 2-D grid:
:param or HTML.:

* **Return type:**
  [`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)]

### ek.totals_consistent(record, , total_key, item_keys, tol=0.01, layer='cross_field')

Flag when `record[total_key]` does not equal the sum of `item_keys` (±tol).

The canonical cross-field check (invoice total = Σ line items). Skipped (rather
than raising or flagging) when the total or *all* item keys are absent or
non-numeric, so it is safe on partial records.

* **Return type:**
  [`Iterable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Iterable)[[`Finding`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Finding)]

### ek.validation_pipeline(\*layers, apply_corrections=True, stop_when=<function \_never_stop>)

Compose validators/correctors into a cheapest -> most-expensive pipeline.

`layers` run in the given order (the order encodes the cost spine). Each layer
is a `(value, *, spec) -> Iterable[Finding]` callable. When `apply_corrections`
(default), the first `CORRECT` finding a layer emits is applied to the value
before the next layer runs – so a cheap deterministic fix is what the expensive
layers then see (the noisy-channel chain). `stop_when` is an injectable
early-exit policy over the findings accumulated so far (see
[`stop_on_correction()`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.stop_on_correction) / [`stop_on_flag()`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.stop_on_flag)); the default runs every layer.

* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[`...`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#Ellipsis), [`ValidationResult`](_autosummary/ek.validate.html.md#ek.validate.ValidationResult)]

### ek.zscore_anomaly_findings(numbers, , field='', threshold=3.5, min_n=30, layer='anomaly')

FLAG numeric values that are robust-z-score outliers (median + MAD based).

A reference-free, **dependency-free** anomaly check that complements
[`benford_findings()`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.benford_findings) (which checks the leading-digit *distribution*; this
checks individual *magnitudes*). For a numeric column it computes each value’s
**modified z-score** – `0.6745 * (x - median) / MAD` – which is robust to the
very outliers it is looking for, and FLAGs those whose absolute score exceeds
`threshold`. One FLAG per outlying value (carrying its index); **FLAG-only** –
it routes a value to review, never edits. Skipped below `min_n` (robust
statistics on a handful of points are noise). When the MAD is 0 (a *near*-constant
column, e.g. many identical values plus one outlier) it falls back to the
mean-absolute-deviation scale (Iglewicz & Hoaglin), so a lone outlier is still
caught; a *truly* constant column (no spread at all) yields no findings. For
*multivariate* outliers, plug an isolation forest via `pyod` (already in
`ek[validation]`) as a custom validator.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)

# _autosummary/ek.metrics.anls.html.md

# ek.metrics.anls

ANLS / ANLS\* (nested-JSON) similarity, wrapping `anls_star`.

ANLS (Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity) is the DocVQA-family metric for a
short answer against acceptable variants: a normalized edit similarity thresholded
at ~0.5 so minor OCR/spelling differences do not zero a correct answer. \*\*ANLS\*\*\*
(Peer et al., 2024, [arXiv 2402.03848](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03848)) generalizes it to *arbitrarily nested*
JSON – strings, tuples (best match), lists (Hungarian matching, penalizing
missing/hallucinated items), and dicts (key-value with penalties for missing or
hallucinated keys) – by mapping both sides to a tree and comparing them. It is the
closest thing to an off-the-shelf nested-JSON IE metric (`misc/docs/ek_02` §3.2).

This wraps the `anls_star` package (Apache-2.0; its only dependency is `munkres`
for the Hungarian matching, and it carries its own pure-Python Levenshtein – no GPL
`Levenshtein` is pulled in). It ships behind the `[metrics]` extra and is
imported lazily, so importing `ek` never requires it.

Because `anls_star` already returns a `[0, 1]` higher-is-better similarity, the
wrapper is thin: it flips `ek`’s `(pred, gold)` argument order to the library’s
`(gt, pred)` order, records the raw similarity in `detail`,
and – for a corpus – [`AnlsMetric.aggregate()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.anls.html.md#ek.metrics.anls.AnlsMetric.aggregate) returns the *mean* ANLS (the “A”
in ANLS: the score is already length-normalized per item, so the corpus statistic is
the average of per-item similarities, unlike CER/WER which accumulate edit counts).

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek.metrics.anls import AnlsMetric
>>> m = AnlsMetric()
>>> round(m("Hello Wrld", "Hello World").value, 3)   # one-char OCR slip
0.909
>>> m({"name": "Acme", "city": "Paris"},
...   {"name": "Acme", "city": "Paris"}).value         # nested, exact
1.0
```

### Classes

| [`AnlsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.anls.html.md#ek.metrics.anls.AnlsMetric)(\*[, threshold])   | ANLS / ANLS\* (nested-JSON) similarity as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric).   |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* ek.metrics.anls.AnlsMetric(, threshold=0.5)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

ANLS / ANLS\* (nested-JSON) similarity as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric).

Handles a bare string (classic ANLS) or an arbitrarily nested
dict/list/tuple/`None` structure (ANLS\*); the backend dispatches on type.

* **Parameters:**
  **threshold** ([`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – ANLS zeroes a per-leaf similarity below this value before
  averaging (the classic ANLS 0.5 cut tolerates minor OCR/spelling
  noise). `anls_star` exposes no parameter for this – it reads a
  class constant `ANLSTree.THRESHOLD` (default `0.5`) – so the metric
  applies the threshold by setting that constant around the call and
  restoring it. **Caveat:** this mutates a process-global, so it is not
  thread-safe; concurrent `AnlsMetric` calls with different thresholds in
  the same process can interfere. Defaults to `0.5`.

#### aggregate(scores)

Corpus ANLS = mean of per-item ANLS (each is already length-normalized).

Unlike CER/WER (which accumulate global edit counts) or field-F1 (micro-TP/
FP/FN), ANLS is defined as the *average* normalized similarity over the
evaluation set – the “A” in ANLS – so the corpus statistic is the plain
mean of the per-item scores.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)


# _autosummary/ek.metrics.fields.html.md

# ek.metrics.fields

Field-level metric for record / dict-shaped extractions.

Compares two flat records key by key into precision / recall / F1, with a wrong
value counting as both a spurious prediction and a missed gold (the conventional
slot-error accounting). It is dependency-free, so it ships in core for the common
“compare these two extracted records” case; the tag-sequence span metrics
(`seqeval` / `nervaluate`, with their *explicit* match schemes) and nested
metrics (ANLS\*) arrive behind the `[metrics]` extra – see `misc/docs/ek_02`.

Aggregation is micro-averaged over the corpus (sum TP/FP/FN, then divide), carried
in each [`Score`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Score)’s `detail` so [`evaluate()`](_autosummary/ek.facade.html.md#ek.facade.evaluate) does it
correctly rather than averaging per-record F1s.

### Classes

| [`FieldMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.fields.html.md#ek.metrics.fields.FieldMetric)(\*[, canonicalizer])   | Per-field precision/recall/F1 for two dict records.   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* ek.metrics.fields.FieldMetric(, canonicalizer=None)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per-field precision/recall/F1 for two dict records.

* **Parameters:**
  **canonicalizer** – Optional `str -> str` applied to string values before
  comparison (e.g. casefold/whitespace folding).

#### aggregate(scores)

Micro-averaged F1 over the corpus (sum TP/FP/FN, then divide).

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)


# _autosummary/ek.metrics.graphs.html.md

# ek.metrics.graphs

The flagship metric: cost-weighted, type-aware distance over a typed graph.

No off-the-shelf library takes a typed schema + per-field/per-type cost weights and
returns a weighted distance over the extracted graph – it is *the* must-build of
this project (see `misc/docs/ek_02` and `misc/docs/ek_06`). The mechanism is a
graph edit distance (GED) whose per-edit costs are supplied by `ek`: relabelling
a node, deleting it, or changing a field each costs an amount read from the Layer-A
[`GraphGrammar`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.GraphGrammar) importance weights. That is how “two extra digits on
a monetary amount” outweighs “a misspelled city” – no hardcoded costs, open-closed
via the schema.

GED is NP-hard; this uses `networkx.graph_edit_distance` with a configurable
`timeout` (it returns the best edit cost found within the budget – an
*approximation* on large graphs), normalizes the distance by the maximum possible
edit cost (delete-all-gold + insert-all-pred), and reports both the normalized
distance (`Score.value`; lower is better) and the derived similarity.

`networkx` ships in the `[metrics]` extra and is imported lazily, so importing
`ek` never pulls it in.

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek import GraphGrammar, NodeType, FieldSpec, TypedGraph, TypedNode
>>> g = GraphGrammar(node_types={"donation": NodeType("donation", fields={
...     "amount": FieldSpec("amount", "number", importance=10.0),
...     "city": FieldSpec("city", "string", importance=1.0)})})
>>> gold = TypedGraph([TypedNode("d1", "donation", {"amount": "100", "city": "Paris"})])
>>> # a wrong amount costs far more than a wrong city, per the schema weights:
>>> wrong_amount = TypedGraph([TypedNode("d1", "donation", {"amount": "900", "city": "Paris"})])
>>> wrong_city = TypedGraph([TypedNode("d1", "donation", {"amount": "100", "city": "Lyon"})])
>>> m = TypedGraphMetric(grammar=g)
>>> m(wrong_amount, gold).detail["raw_distance"]
10.0
>>> m(wrong_city, gold).detail["raw_distance"]
1.0
```

### Module Attributes

| [`DEFAULT_MAX_NODES`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.graphs.html.md#ek.metrics.graphs.DEFAULT_MAX_NODES)   | graph edit distance is NP-hard, so a larger pair is rejected (raise) rather than silently spinning.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| [`TypedGraphMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.graphs.html.md#ek.metrics.graphs.TypedGraphMetric)([grammar, weights, ...]) | Cost-weighted, type-aware typed-graph edit distance as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric). |
| [`TypedNode`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.graphs.html.md#ek.metrics.graphs.TypedNode)(node_id, node_type[, fields])   | A node in a typed graph: an id, a node-type tag, and its field values.                                                           |

# _autosummary/ek.metrics.html.md

# ek.metrics

Reference-based (offline) metrics: the `score()` side of `ek`.

A [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) compares one prediction to one gold reference and
returns a [`Score`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Score). The *right* metric is a function of the output
**object type** – a string wants CER/WER, a record wants field-level F1, a table
wants TEDS/GriTS, a typed graph wants a cost-weighted edit distance. This package
holds the concrete metrics and registers each under the `"metrics"` namespace so
the [`score()`](_autosummary/ek.facade.html.md#ek.facade.score) facade can dispatch by type or by name.

Shipping in core (zero/low-dependency): [`StringMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.html.md#ek.metrics.StringMetric) (CER/WER, via
`jiwer` when present) and [`FieldMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.html.md#ek.metrics.FieldMetric) (record/dict field F1). The richer
metrics ship behind the `[metrics]` extra and import their backends lazily, so
constructing or registering them never pulls a heavy dependency:

- [`AnlsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.anls.html.md#ek.metrics.anls.AnlsMetric) – ANLS / ANLS\* (nested-JSON), via `anls_star`.
- [`SpanF1Metric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.SpanF1Metric) – span/slot P/R/F1 via `seqeval` AND
  `nervaluate`, under an **explicit, required** [`MatchScheme`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme).
- [`TedsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.TedsMetric) / [`GritsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.GritsMetric) –
  table-structure metrics (TEDS/TEDS-Struct, GriTS-Top/GriTS-Con) with a
  `structure_only` toggle.
- [`TypedGraphMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.graphs.html.md#ek.metrics.graphs.TypedGraphMetric) – the flagship cost-weighted typed
  graph edit distance.

See `misc/docs/ek_02` (the reference-based decision table and gotchas).

### Classes

### *class* ek.metrics.AnlsMetric(, threshold=0.5)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

ANLS / ANLS\* (nested-JSON) similarity as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric).

Handles a bare string (classic ANLS) or an arbitrarily nested
dict/list/tuple/`None` structure (ANLS\*); the backend dispatches on type.

* **Parameters:**
  **threshold** ([`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – ANLS zeroes a per-leaf similarity below this value before
  averaging (the classic ANLS 0.5 cut tolerates minor OCR/spelling
  noise). `anls_star` exposes no parameter for this – it reads a
  class constant `ANLSTree.THRESHOLD` (default `0.5`) – so the metric
  applies the threshold by setting that constant around the call and
  restoring it. **Caveat:** this mutates a process-global, so it is not
  thread-safe; concurrent `AnlsMetric` calls with different thresholds in
  the same process can interfere. Defaults to `0.5`.

#### aggregate(scores)

Corpus ANLS = mean of per-item ANLS (each is already length-normalized).

Unlike CER/WER (which accumulate global edit counts) or field-F1 (micro-TP/
FP/FN), ANLS is defined as the *average* normalized similarity over the
evaluation set – the “A” in ANLS – so the corpus statistic is the plain
mean of the per-item scores.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### *class* ek.metrics.GritsMetric(, structure_only=False)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

GriTS-Top / GriTS-Con as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) (pure-Python, P/R aware).

* **Parameters:**
  **structure_only** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – When `True`, score cell topology only (GriTS-Top); when
  `False` (default), average topology with cell-content similarity
  (GriTS-Con).

Corpus GriTS F1: pool overlap and per-table cell counts, then divide once.

GriTS precision = overlap / 

```
|pred cells|
```

 and recall = overlap / 

```
|gold cells|
```

;
the corpus statistic micro-averages by summing the numerators and

# _autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md

# ek.metrics.spans

Span / slot precision-recall-F1 over two backends that legitimately disagree.

Entity/slot F1 is the workhorse for fields-and-spans extraction, but a *single* F1
is meaningless without naming its **match scheme** – and the two standard backends
diverge widely *and disagree with each other* (`misc/docs/ek_02` §2.2):

- **seqeval** (MIT, `chakki-works`) – CoNLL `conlleval`-compatible entity F1
  over BIO/IOBES tag *sequences*. Its `conll` (default) and `strict` (span+type,
  keyed to a tagging scheme) modes are the reference for sequence-labelling NER.
- **nervaluate** (MIT, `MantisAI`) – the SemEval-2013 Task 9.1 scheme over typed
  *spans*, with four schemas: **strict** (span + type), **exact** (span, any type),
  **partial** (boundary overlap, any type), **type** (type with span overlap). It
  counts COR/INC/PAR/MIS/SPU and gives partial spans half credit.

A model that finds “Electric” instead of “General Electric” scores F1=0 under
exact-span matching but ~0.667 under a partial/token scheme – so the scheme is *not*
a default you can hide. This module makes [`MatchScheme`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme) a **required keyword**
with no default: you must say which contract you are scoring under.

Both backends ship behind the `[metrics]` extra and are imported lazily, so
importing `ek` never pulls them in. Each [`Score`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Score) carries the raw
TP/FP/FN (or COR/INC/PAR/MIS/SPU) counts in its `detail` so
[`SpanF1Metric.aggregate()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.SpanF1Metric.aggregate) micro-averages over a corpus – never a naive mean of
per-document F1s.

## Input shapes

- `seqeval` schemes ([`MatchScheme.SEQEVAL_CONLL`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme.SEQEVAL_CONLL),
  [`MatchScheme.SEQEVAL_STRICT`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme.SEQEVAL_STRICT)): `pred` and `gold` are **tag sequences** –
  > a list of BIO/IOBES tags (e.g. `["B-PER", "I-PER", "O"]`).
- `nervaluate` schemes ([`MatchScheme.STRICT`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme.STRICT), `EXACT`, `PARTIAL`,
  `TYPE`): `pred` and `gold` are **span lists** – a list of
  `{"label", "start", "end"}` dicts.

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek.metrics.spans import SpanF1Metric, MatchScheme
>>> m = SpanF1Metric(scheme=MatchScheme.SEQEVAL_CONLL)
>>> s = m(["B-PER", "I-PER", "O"], ["B-PER", "I-PER", "O"])
>>> s.f1
1.0
>>> SpanF1Metric()
Traceback (most recent call last):
TypeError: SpanF1Metric requires an explicit scheme=MatchScheme.<...>
```

### Classes

| [`MatchScheme`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme)(\*values)                  | The (backend, scheme) contract a span/slot F1 is computed under.                                                    |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`SpanF1Metric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.SpanF1Metric)([scheme, tagging_scheme]) | Entity/slot precision/recall/F1 under an **explicit** [`MatchScheme`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.spans.html.md#ek.metrics.spans.MatchScheme). |

The two backends legitimately disagree (seqeval ignores other-type tags at the

SemEval-2013 *span lists* via nervaluate.

#### EXACT *= 'exact'*

exact span boundaries, type ignored.

* **Type:**
  nervaluate exact

#### PARTIAL *= 'partial'*

boundary *overlap* (half credit), type ignored.

* **Type:**
  nervaluate partial

#### SEQEVAL_CONLL *= 'seqeval_conll'*

seqeval, CoNLL `conlleval`-compatible entity F1 (the default seqeval mode).

#### SEQEVAL_STRICT *= 'seqeval_strict'*

span boundaries AND type must match, keyed to a scheme.

  seqeval strict mode

#### STRICT *= 'strict'*

# _autosummary/ek.metrics.strings.html.md

# ek.metrics.strings

String metrics: Character/Word Error Rate (CER/WER).

CER and WER are graded edit-distance metrics – the right baseline for OCR/ASR and
free-text fields, far less brittle than exact match. Two correctness rules from the
research drive the design:

1. **Accumulate globally.** A corpus error rate is `sum(edits) / sum(reference
   length)` over the whole corpus – never the mean of per-item rates (variable
   lengths make that mathematically wrong). So each [`Score`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Score) carries
   raw `edits` and `ref_len` in its `detail`, and [`StringMetric.aggregate()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.strings.html.md#ek.metrics.strings.StringMetric.aggregate)
   sums them. [`evaluate()`](_autosummary/ek.facade.html.md#ek.facade.evaluate) uses this.
2. **CER/WER are error rates, not bounded similarities.** A hypothesis longer than
   the reference pushes the rate above 1.0 – itself a useful hallucination signal.
   `Score.value` is the error rate (lower is better; `detail["higher_is_better"]
   is False`).

The canonical backend is `jiwer` (Apache-2.0, `rapidfuzz` C++ core), which also
yields the substitution/deletion/insertion/hit breakdown. `ek` prefers it,
falls back to `rapidfuzz` directly, then to a pure-Python edit distance, so the
metric works even in a bare environment.

### Classes

| [`StringMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.strings.html.md#ek.metrics.strings.StringMetric)([mode, canonicalizer])   | CER (`mode='cer'`) or WER (`mode='wer'`) as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric).   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

### *class* ek.metrics.strings.StringMetric(mode='cer', , canonicalizer=None)

# _autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md

# ek.metrics.tables

Table-structure metrics: TEDS / TEDS-Struct and GriTS (structure-only toggle).

Two complementary table-recognition metrics from `misc/docs/ek_02` §3.1:

- **TEDS** (Tree-Edit-Distance-based Similarity; Zhong et al., PubTabNet, IBM,
  [arXiv 1911.10683](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.10683)) renders a table as an HTML tree and scores
  `1 - EditDist(Ta, Tb) / max(|Ta|, |Tb|)`. It captures both *structure* and
  *cell content*. **TEDS-Struct** (the `structure_only=True` toggle) ignores cell
  text to isolate structure, since “taking OCR errors into account may lead to an
  unfair comparison due to the different OCR models used by various TSR methods”.
- **GriTS** (Grid Table Similarity; Smock et al., Microsoft, [arXiv 2203.12555](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.12555))
  scores the predicted table directly as a 2-D matrix and yields **precision/recall**
  over the most-similar common sub-grid. Its **GriTS-Top** (topology, structure-only)
  and **GriTS-Con** (content) variants share the `structure_only` toggle.

Licensing note (`skills/ek-dev-licensing`): the obvious wrapper target,
`table-recognition-metric`, pulls in the **GPL** `Levenshtein` package as a hard
runtime dependency (`from Levenshtein import distance` in its source) – a
scanner-invisible copyleft landmine that would fail the CI license gate. So TEDS is
implemented **clean-room** here on the MIT `apted` engine (already in
`[metrics]`), and GriTS is a dependency-free pure-Python implementation of the
2D-MSS heuristic. Both follow the precedent of reimplementing Krippendorff’s alpha in
pure Python rather than quarantining a copyleft dependency.

## Input shapes

`pred` and `gold` are [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) objects, or anything the constructors
accept: an HTML `str` (`<table>...</table>`; via [`Table.from_html()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table.from_html)) or a
2-D grid – a list of rows of cell strings, where `None` marks a cell spanned over
by a neighbour (via [`Table.from_grid()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table.from_grid)). The facade and registry coerce HTML
strings automatically.

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek.metrics.tables import TedsMetric, GritsMetric, Table
>>> a = "<table><tr><td>a</td><td>b</td></tr></table>"
>>> b = "<table><tr><td>a</td><td>c</td></tr></table>"
>>> round(TedsMetric()(a, b).value, 3)            # one cell-content edit
0.75
>>> TedsMetric(structure_only=True)(a, b).value   # same structure -> 1.0
1.0
>>> GritsMetric(structure_only=True)(a, b).value  # identical grid topology
1.0
```

### Classes

| [`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell)([text, rowspan, colspan])    | One logical table cell: its text plus its row/column span (>=1 each).                                                       |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`GritsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.GritsMetric)(\*[, structure_only]) | GriTS-Top / GriTS-Con as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) (pure-Python, P/R aware). |
| [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)([rows])                     | A table as an ordered list of rows of [`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell) s (the logical cells).          |
| [`TedsMetric`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.TedsMetric)(\*[, structure_only])  | TEDS / TEDS-Struct as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) (clean-room on `apted`).     |

### *class* ek.metrics.tables.Cell(text='', rowspan=1, colspan=1)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One logical table cell: its text plus its row/column span (>=1 each).

### *class* ek.metrics.tables.GritsMetric(, structure_only=False)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

GriTS-Top / GriTS-Con as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) (pure-Python, P/R aware).

* **Parameters:**
  **structure_only** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – When `True`, score cell topology only (GriTS-Top); when
  `False` (default), average topology with cell-content similarity
  (GriTS-Con).

#### aggregate(scores)

Corpus GriTS F1: pool overlap and per-table cell counts, then divide once.

GriTS precision = overlap / 

```
|pred cells|
```

 and recall = overlap / 

```
|gold cells|
```

;
the corpus statistic micro-averages by summing the numerators and
denominators globally – never a mean of per-table F1s.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

### *class* ek.metrics.tables.Table(rows=())

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

A table as an ordered list of rows of [`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell) s (the logical cells).

`rows[i]` is the i-th row’s logical cells in reading order; spans are carried
on each [`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell). Use [`from_html()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table.from_html) / [`from_grid()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table.from_grid) to build one,
and [`as_grid()`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table.as_grid) for the dense 2-D occupancy view GriTS scores.

#### as_grid()

Expand spans into a dense 2-D grid; a spanned position repeats its cell.

Each physical grid position holds the (shared) [`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell) covering it, so
two tables with the same topology have grids of the same shape – the view
GriTS aligns position-by-position.

* **Return type:**
  [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)[[`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Cell`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Cell)]]]

#### *classmethod* coerce(obj)

Coerce a [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table), an HTML string, or a 2-D grid into a Table.

* **Return type:**
  [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)

#### *classmethod* from_grid(grid)

Build a Table from a 2-D grid of cell texts (`None` = spanned-over).

* **Return type:**
  [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)

#### *classmethod* from_html(html)

Parse an HTML `<table>` (with `colspan`/`rowspan`) into a Table.

* **Return type:**
  [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)

### *class* ek.metrics.tables.TedsMetric(, structure_only=False)

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

TEDS / TEDS-Struct as a [`Metric`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Metric) (clean-room on `apted`).

* **Parameters:**
  **structure_only** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – When `True`, ignore cell text and score structure alone
  (TEDS-Struct), isolating table-structure accuracy from OCR noise.
  Defaults to `False` (full TEDS: structure + content).

#### aggregate(scores)

Corpus TEDS = **mean** of per-table TEDS (the PubTabNet/OmniDocBench
convention). Each per-table TEDS is already node-count-normalized, so the
reported corpus statistic is the average, not a pooled edit-rate. The pooled
`1 - sum(dist)/sum(nodes)` is available from the per-item `detail` if a
size-weighted variant is wanted instead.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)


# _autosummary/ek.ocr.benchmark.html.md

# ek.ocr.benchmark

End-to-end OCR offline benchmark: run a fleet over gold, score, persist.

This is `ek`’s first out-of-the-box experience – “how accurate is my OCR?”. It
pairs each gold item with the engine’s output, scores text with a globally
accumulated CER/WER (the correct corpus aggregation), optionally slices the report,
and persists gold + per-item results + the run aggregate to the `dol` stores
under `~/.local/share/ek/`.

The runner is deliberately source-agnostic: `engine` is any
`image -> OcrResult` callable (or an `ocracy` backend id, bridged for you), so
the benchmark runs – and is fully testable – without any real OCR engine or cloud
credentials.

### Example

```pycon
>>> import tempfile; root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
>>> gold = {
...     "d1": {"image": "ignored", "reference_text": "cat", "slice": "easy"},
...     "d2": {"image": "ignored", "reference_text": "dog", "slice": "easy"},
... }
>>> # a stub engine that always reads "cat" (perfect for d1, wrong for d2):
>>> engine = lambda image: type("R", (), {"text": "cat"})()
>>> report = evaluate_ocr(engine, gold, metric="cer", rootdir=root)
>>> report.n
2
>>> sorted(report.per_slice)
['easy']
```

### Functions

| [`add_gold_item`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.benchmark.html.md#ek.ocr.benchmark.add_gold_item)(key, image, reference_text, \*)   | Add one gold example to the `gold` store.      |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| [`evaluate_ocr`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.benchmark.html.md#ek.ocr.benchmark.evaluate_ocr)(engine, gold, \*[, metric, ...])   | Benchmark an OCR engine against a gold corpus. |

### ek.ocr.benchmark.add_gold_item(key, image, reference_text, , slice=None, rootdir=None, \*\*extra)

Add one gold example to the `gold` store.

* **Parameters:**
  * **key** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Unique id for the document.
  * **image** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – An image reference the engine can read (path, URL, …). Stored as a
    reference, not bytes – gold stores hold references + the expected text.
  * **reference_text** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The ground-truth transcription.
  * **slice** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Optional stratification label (doc type, language, scan quality, …).
  * **rootdir** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Override the data root (tests/ephemeral use).
  * **\*\*extra** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Any additional metadata to store on the record.
* **Return type:**
  [`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None)

### ek.ocr.benchmark.evaluate_ocr(engine, gold, , metric='cer', normalize=None, grammar=None, image_key='image', reference_key='reference_text', slice_key='slice', persist=False, run_id=None, rootdir=None)

Benchmark an OCR engine against a gold corpus.

* **Parameters:**
  * **engine** ([`Union`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Union)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)]) – An `image -> OcrResult` callable, or an `ocracy` backend id.
  * **gold** ([`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)) – A mapping `key -> {image, reference_text, [slice], ...}` – a plain
    dict or a `ek` gold store.
  * **metric** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – `"cer"` (default) or `"wer"` (or any registered string metric).
  * **normalize** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Optional canonicalizer applied to both sides before scoring.
  * **grammar** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Optional Layer-A grammar (forwarded to the metric).
  * **image_key** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Field names within each gold record.
  * **reference_key** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Field names within each gold record.
  * **slice_key** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Field names within each gold record.
  * **persist** ([`bool`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – If true, write per-item results and the run aggregate to the
    `results` / `runs` stores.
  * **run_id** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Identifier for this run (auto-generated from the clock if omitted).
  * **rootdir** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Override the data root (tests/ephemeral use).
* **Returns:**
  A [`Report`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Report) whose `detail['per_item']` maps each gold key to
  its prediction, reference, slice, score, and engine confidence/backend.


# _autosummary/ek.ocr.bridge.html.md

# ek.ocr.bridge

The `ocracy` bridge: turn the OCR fleet into an `image -> OcrResult` callable.

`ocracy` is a deliberately dependency-free facade over ~16 OCR engines whose
single entry point `ocracy.ocr(image, *, backend=None, **kwargs)` returns a
normalized `OcrResult` (`.text` plus `.blocks` carrying `[0, 1]`-normalized
confidence and geometry). `ek` consumes that shape rather than reinventing engine
integration. The bridge is intentionally tiny – it only adapts `ocracy`’s call
into the [`OcrBackend`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.OcrBackend) contract and guards the optional dependency
with an actionable install hint.

Null-safety reminder (see `misc/docs/ek_01`): VLM/markdown engines (Claude,
GPT-4o, Mistral OCR) return text only – `blocks == []` and `confidence is
None`. Any code reading confidence/geometry off the result must tolerate `None`.

### Functions

| [`ocracy_backend`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.bridge.html.md#ek.ocr.bridge.ocracy_backend)([backend])       | Return an `image -> OcrResult` callable bound to one `ocracy` backend.   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`read_text`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.bridge.html.md#ek.ocr.bridge.read_text)(image, \*[, backend]) | Convenience: OCR an image and return just the recognized text string.    |

### ek.ocr.bridge.ocracy_backend(backend=None, \*\*default_kwargs)

Return an `image -> OcrResult` callable bound to one `ocracy` backend.

* **Parameters:**
  * **backend** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – An `ocracy` backend id (e.g. `"tesseract"`, `"google_vision"`);
    `None` uses `ocracy`’s first installed backend.
  * **\*\*default_kwargs** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Options forwarded to `ocracy.ocr` on every call
    (e.g. `languages=["en"]`); per-call kwargs override these.
* **Return type:**
  [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]
* **Returns:**
  A callable suitable for [`ek.ocr.evaluate_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.evaluate_ocr).

### ek.ocr.bridge.read_text(image, , backend=None, \*\*kwargs)

Convenience: OCR an image and return just the recognized text string.

* **Return type:**
  [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)


# _autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md

# ek.ocr

OCR evaluation – `ek`’s first concrete instance, built on `ocracy`.

OCR is the noisiest special case of information extraction. This subpackage adds
the OCR-specific pieces on top of `ek`’s source-agnostic core:

- [`ocracy_backend()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.ocracy_backend) / [`read_text()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.read_text) – a thin bridge that turns
  `ocracy`’s 16-engine fleet into an `image -> OcrResult` callable. The
  dependency arrow is strict: `ek -> ocracy` (via the `ek[ocr]` extra), never
  the reverse. `ek` core depends only on the `OcrResult` *shape* (`.text` /
  `.blocks` / `.mean_confidence`), so the benchmark below evaluates *any*
  `image -> OcrResult` callable – `ocracy` or your own.
- [`profile()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.profile) – per-engine capability profiles (who emits real vs
  model-guessed geometry, who is calibrated, who yields table structure), distilled
  from `misc/docs/ek_01`. `ek` treats these as claims to verify empirically.
- [`evaluate_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.evaluate_ocr) / [`add_gold_item()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.add_gold_item) – run a fleet over a gold corpus,
  score with CER/WER (globally accumulated), slice the report, and persist gold +
  results to the `dol` stores under `~/.local/share/ek/`.
- [`table_from_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.table_from_ocr) / [`has_table_structure()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.has_table_structure) – recover the existing
  [`ek.metrics.tables.Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) from an `OcrResult` (whose engine-specific table
  > data lives only in `.raw`/`.markdown`) so the table metrics (TEDS / GriTS) can
  > score OCR table output uniformly. The per-engine extractor is injected/registered
  > under the `"table_parsers"` namespace (open-closed); see [`ek.ocr.tables`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.tables.html.md#module-ek.ocr.tables).

Heavy engine SDKs and credentials are never required to import this module; they
are checked at call time via [`ek.registry.check_requirements()`](_autosummary/ek.registry.html.md#ek.registry.check_requirements).

### Functions

| [`ocracy_backend`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.ocracy_backend)([backend])                     | Return an `image -> OcrResult` callable bound to one `ocracy` backend.                                                   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`read_text`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.read_text)(image, \*[, backend])               | Convenience: OCR an image and return just the recognized text string.                                                    |
| [`evaluate_ocr`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.evaluate_ocr)(engine, gold, \*[, metric, ...]) | Benchmark an OCR engine against a gold corpus.                                                                           |
| [`add_gold_item`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.add_gold_item)(key, image, reference_text, \*) | Add one gold example to the `gold` store.                                                                                |
| [`profile`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.profile)(engine)                               | Capability profile for an engine id (a safe default if unknown).                                                         |
| [`table_from_ocr`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.table_from_ocr)(ocr_result, \*[, parser])      | Extract a normalized [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) from an `OcrResult`. |
| [`has_table_structure`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.has_table_structure)(ocr_result, \*[, parser]) | Whether [`table_from_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.table_from_ocr) recovers a non-empty table from `ocr_result`.  |
| [`resolve_table_parser`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.resolve_table_parser)(ref)                     | Resolve a table parser reference (a registered name or a callable) to a callable.                                        |
| [`engine_yields_tables`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.engine_yields_tables)(engine)                  | Whether `engine`'s capability profile claims scoreable table structure.                                                  |

  * **key** ([`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – Unique id for the document.
  * **image** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – An image reference the engine can read (path, URL, …). Stored as a

### ek.ocr.engine_yields_tables(engine)

Whether `engine`’s capability profile claims scoreable table structure.

A convenience over [`ek.ocr.profile()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.profile): returns the engine profile’s `tables`
flag. ek treats the profile as a *prior* (Azure DI, AWS Textract, PaddleOCR and the
markdown engines are expected to yield scoreable tables; Google Vision is not), to
be verified empirically by actually running [`table_from_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.table_from_ocr). Use it to skip
table scoring for engines that cannot emit cells in the first place.

* **Return type:**

  * **run_id** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Identifier for this run (auto-generated from the clock if omitted).
  * **rootdir** ([`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)]) – Override the data root (tests/ephemeral use).
* **Returns:**

  its prediction, reference, slice, score, and engine confidence/backend.

### ek.ocr.table_from_ocr(ocr_result, , parser=None)

Extract a normalized [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) from an `OcrResult`.

The single seam ek’s table metrics (TEDS / GriTS) use to score OCR table output
uniformly. Returns the recovered Table, or `None` when the result carries no
recoverable table structure.

* **Parameters:**
  * **ocr_result** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Any `OcrResult`-shaped object. ek reads only its `.raw` (the
    engine-specific payload), `.markdown` (VLM/markdown engines), and
    `.meta` – never ocracy types, so any `image -> OcrResult` callable’s
    output works.
  * **parser** ([`Union`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Union)[[`None`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/constants.html#None), [`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]]) – 

    How to turn the raw payload into a table (dependency injection /
    open-closed). One of:
    - `None` (default): try the built-in **safe heuristics** – `.raw` is
      already a [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table), a 2-D grid, or a
      `<table>...</table>` HTML string; or `.raw`/`.meta` is a mapping
      carrying one of `{tables, table, cells, grid, html}`; or `.markdown`
      contains an HTML `<table>`. Returns `None` if none match – it never
      guesses wildly.
    - a `str`: the name of a parser registered under `"table_parsers"`
      (per-engine extractor), resolved from [`ek.registry`](_autosummary/ek.registry.html.md#module-ek.registry).
    - a callable `(raw) -> Table | grid | html | None`: an inline per-engine
      extractor. It receives the result’s `.raw` (falling back to the result
      itself when there is no `.raw`).
  * **through** (*Any non-None value an injected parser returns is fed*)
* **Return type:**
  [*Table*](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) | *None*

:param `Table.coerce()`:
:param so a parser may yield a Table:
:param a 2-D grid:
:param or HTML.:

* **Return type:**
  [`Optional`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Optional)[[`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table)]
* **Returns:**
  A non-empty [`Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table), or `None` when no table
  structure is recoverable. An empty Table (no rows/cells) is normalized to
  `None` so the predicate [`has_table_structure()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.html.md#ek.ocr.has_table_structure) and downstream metrics
  see “no table”, not a degenerate one.

# _autosummary/ek.ocr.profiles.html.md

# ek.ocr.profiles

Per-engine OCR capability profiles (what QE signal each engine actually emits).

Distilled from the 15-engine inventory in `misc/docs/ek_01`. These describe what
an engine *claims* to surface; `ek` exists in part to verify such claims
empirically, so treat them as defaults/priors, not ground truth. The fields that
matter for evaluation:

- `confidence_grain` – finest confidence granularity emitted: `"symbol"` >
  `"word"` > `"line"` > `"none"`. Genuine per-symbol confidence exists only
  in Google Cloud Vision and Tesseract; many VLMs emit nothing usable.
- `has_real_provenance` – whether bounding boxes are real geometry (vs
  model-guessed pixels from Claude/OpenAI, or char-offset only from Mistral).
- `calibrated` – whether the confidence is calibrated (Mathpix is the lone
  calibrated emitter).
- `tables` – whether the engine emits scoreable table cell structure.

### Example

```pycon
>>> profile("tesseract")["confidence_grain"]
'symbol'
>>> profile("claude-vision")["has_real_provenance"]
False
>>> profile("google_vision")["confidence_grain"]   # underscore form also accepted
'symbol'
>>> profile("totally-unknown-engine")["confidence_grain"]
'unknown'
```

|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| [`DEFAULT_PROFILE`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.profiles.html.md#ek.ocr.profiles.DEFAULT_PROFILE)   | Returned for any engine not in the table. |

|--------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|

# _autosummary/ek.ocr.tables.html.md

# ek.ocr.tables

Recover a normalized table from an `OcrResult` so ek’s table metrics can score it.

`ocracy` exposes **no** normalized table/cell type: `TextBlock.level` stops at
`block`, with no cell/row/column model, so OCR table structure survives only inside
the engine-specific `OcrResult.raw` (Textract `Block` objects, PaddleOCR
`pred_html`, Azure `tables[]`) or in the markdown/HTML an engine emits
(`res.markdown` for VLM engines). ek therefore can’t uniformly score table
structure (TEDS / GriTS) off the `OcrResult` shape alone.

This module is the **ek-side seam** that closes that gap *without touching ocracy*
(the dependency arrow stays `ek -> ocracy`, never the reverse). It turns an
`OcrResult`-shaped object into the existing [`ek.metrics.tables.Table`](_autosummary/ek.metrics.tables.html.md#ek.metrics.tables.Table) (the
one TEDS/GriTS already score) – it does **not** define a new table type.

Because every engine stores tables differently, the per-engine extractor is an
**injected** callable (open-closed / dependency-injection): pass `parser=` a
`(raw) -> Table | grid | html | None` function, or register one under the
`"table_parsers"` namespace and pass its name. With no parser,
[`table_from_ocr()`](_autosummary/ek.ocr.tables.html.md#ek.ocr.tables.table_from_ocr) falls back to a few **safe, documented** heuristics over the
result’s `raw`/`markdown`/`meta` and returns `None` when no table structure is
present – it never guesses wildly.

Nothing here imports `ocracy` or any OCR engine: ek depends only on the
`OcrResult` *shape* (`.text` / `.raw` / `.markdown` / `.meta`), so this works
on any `image -> OcrResult` callable’s output.

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek.metrics.tables import Table
>>> class R:  # a minimal OcrResult-shaped object carrying a 2-D grid in .raw
...     raw = {"tables": [[["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]]]}
>>> t = table_from_ocr(R())
>>> [[c.text for c in row] for row in t.rows]
[['a', 'b'], ['c', 'd']]
>>> has_table_structure(R())
True
>>> class Empty:  # no table anywhere in the result
...     raw = {"text": "just prose"}
>>> table_from_ocr(Empty()) is None
True
```

A registered third-party engine parser, used by name:

```pycon
>>> from ek.registry import register
>>> @register("table_parsers", "demo")
... def _demo(raw):
...     return raw.get("cells")  # this engine stores a grid under raw['cells']
>>> class D:
...     raw = {"cells": [["x"]]}
>>> table_from_ocr(D(), parser="demo").rows[0][0].text
'x'
```

|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|

# _autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md

# ek.qe.calibrate

Calibration: make a raw score *mean* a probability (the non-optional stage).

A confidence of 0.9 should mean “correct 90% of the time.” Modern models violate
this badly – they are systematically **overconfident** (Guo et al. 2017), and RLHF
makes LLMs worse. So \*\*calibration is non-optional: never gate a raw posterior or a
raw logprob\*\* (`misc/docs/ek_03` §2, Hard Rule 1). A [`Calibrator`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Calibrator)
is fit on a labelled holdout of `(raw_score, field_correct?)` pairs and maps any
later raw score to a calibrated probability.

Three methods, by what input you have:

- [`PlattCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator) – logistic fit on any scalar score (no logits needed):
  **the default** for aggregated OCR confidence or aggregated logprobs.
- [`IsotonicCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.IsotonicCalibrator) – non-parametric monotonic fit; more flexible, needs
  more data, can overfit small sets.
- [`TemperatureCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.TemperatureCalibrator) – a single scalar `T` on **logits**; use only
  when you have logits (it does not change the argmax).

All three are pure-Python (stdlib only) so the calibration stage works with zero
extra dependencies; [`sklearn_calibrator()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.sklearn_calibrator) / `netcal_calibrator()` offer the
library-backed equivalents behind the `ek[calibration]` extra. Measure calibration
with [`expected_calibration_error()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.expected_calibration_error) (+ a reliability curve). For per-field-type
validity, wrap per group with [`GroupCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.GroupCalibrator) (Mondrian / class-conditional)
– distribution-free *conditional* coverage is otherwise impossible (Hard Rule 2).
When the raw signals are *heterogeneous* (a judge score next to a logprob next to a
ROVER agreement), calibrate each signal family on its own with
[`SignalFamilyCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator) and fuse the calibrated probabilities with a
documented combiner ([`mean_probability()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.mean_probability) by default, [`min_probability()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.min_probability)
for a conservative gate), rather than calibrating the mean of incomparable scores.

Calibrate at the **granularity of the decision** (gate on fields -> calibrate a
“field-correct?” target), and persist the fit ([`save_calibrator()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.save_calibrator)); calibration
is dataset-specific and decays, so re-fit on drift.

### Example

```pycon
>>> # An overconfident raw signal, calibrated against ground truth.
>>> raw =     [0.95, 0.93, 0.92, 0.90, 0.55, 0.52, 0.51, 0.50]
>>> correct = [True, True, False, False, True, False, False, False]
>>> cal = PlattCalibrator().fit(raw, correct)
>>> cal(0.95) < 0.95            # overconfidence pulled down
True
>>> 0.0 <= cal(0.5) <= 1.0
True
```

### Module Attributes

| [`DEFAULT_N_BINS`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.DEFAULT_N_BINS)   | Default number of bins for [`expected_calibration_error()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.expected_calibration_error) / reliability curves.   |

### *class* ek.qe.calibrate.GroupCalibrator(factory=<class 'ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator'>, by_group=dict(), pooled=None, kind='group')

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Per-group (Mondrian) calibration: one calibrator per `NodeType`/`FieldSpec`.

Distribution-free *conditional* (per-field-type) coverage is impossible
in general (Barber et al. 2019); calibrating separately per group restores it
approximately. `fit` takes a parallel `groups` sequence; `__call__` routes
by group key, falling back to a pooled calibrator for unseen groups.

* **Parameters:**
  **factory** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – Zero-arg callable producing a fresh per-group calibrator (default
  [`PlattCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator)).

#### factory

alias of [`PlattCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator)

#### fit(scores, correct, , groups)

Fit one calibrator per distinct group key, plus a pooled fallback.

* **Return type:**
  [`GroupCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.GroupCalibrator)

#### to_dict()

Serialize each per-group calibrator (keyed by stringified group) plus the
pooled fallback, so a fitted Mondrian calibrator round-trips like the others.
Group keys are stringified (they are `NodeType`/`FieldSpec` names).

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### *class* ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator(a=1.0, b=0.0, max_iter=100, kind='platt')

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

Platt scaling: `sigmoid(a * score + b)`, fit by Newton/IRLS on labels.

The default calibrator: works on any scalar (aggregated confidence/logprob), no
logits required. Uses Platt’s target smoothing so it does not overfit small
calibration sets.

* **Parameters:**
  **max_iter** ([`int`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Newton iterations (converges in a handful for a 2-parameter model).

#### fit(scores, correct)

Fit `a, b` to maximise the likelihood of `correct` given `scores`.

* **Return type:**
  [`PlattCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator)

### *class* ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator(calibrators=dict(), combine=<function mean_probability>, factory=<class 'ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator'>, fusion=None, kind='signal_family')

Bases: [`object`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#object)

One calibrator per signal family, fused by a documented combination rule.

Averaging heterogeneous raw signals (an LLM-judge score, a token logprob, a ROVER
agreement) and calibrating the mean discards exactly what a calibrator needs:
each family has its own scale, reliability and direction of miscalibration. This
calibrates every signal *by name* with its own calibrator, then fuses the
calibrated probabilities with `combine`.

Pass it (or simply a `Mapping[str, Calibrator]`) as
`estimate_quality(..., calibrator=...)`.

**The fused value must itself be calibrated before it is gated.** Fusing
calibrated probabilities (by mean, min, …) does not yield a calibrated
probability: agreeing families make the mean under-confident, a weak family
drags it toward the base rate. So [`fit()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator.fit) also learns a second-stage
`fusion` calibrator on `combine`’s output, and `__call__` applies it.
Without a `fusion` calibrator (e.g. a hand-built mapping),
[`ek.estimate_quality()`](_autosummary/ek.html.md#ek.estimate_quality) refuses to gate a value fused from two or more
families unless told `assume_calibrated=True` (Hard Rule 1). A value from a
single family is that family’s calibrated probability and gates as is.

A field’s own upstream `confidence` is just one more family here, named
`"confidence"`: include it in the training rows under that name.

* **Parameters:**
  * **calibrators** ([`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)) – `signal name -> Calibrator`. A `"*"` entry is the fallback
    for any signal without its own entry. A signal with neither is refused
    (`ValueError`) rather than silently dropped or passed through raw
    (Hard Rule 1).
  * **combine** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[[`Mapping`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)[[`str`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str), [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]], [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)]) – `Mapping[str, float] -> float` fusing the calibrated values;
    [`mean_probability()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.mean_probability) (default) or [`min_probability()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.min_probability), or any
    callable of that shape (e.g. a learned stacker).
  * **factory** ([`Callable`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Callable)[[], [`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)]) – Zero-arg callable producing a fresh calibrator, used by [`fit()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator.fit).
  * **fusion** ([`Any`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Any)) – Second-stage calibrator applied to `combine`’s output (learned by
    [`fit()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator.fit)); `None` leaves the fused value uncalibrated.

### Example

```pycon
>>> rows = [{"judge": j, "logprob": l} for j, l in
...         [(0.9, -0.1), (0.8, -0.2), (0.85, -2.0), (0.3, -0.1), (0.2, -2.5), (0.7, -1.8)]]
>>> correct = [True, True, False, True, False, False]
>>> cal = SignalFamilyCalibrator().fit(rows, correct)
>>> sorted(cal.calibrators)
['judge', 'logprob']
>>> 0.0 <= cal({"judge": 0.9, "logprob": -0.1}) <= 1.0
True
```

#### calibrate_signals(raw_signals, , group=None)

`{name: calibrated probability}` for each raw signal (before fusion).

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

#### combine()

Fuse calibrated per-family probabilities by their mean (the default combiner).

Each family’s calibrated value estimates the *same* event (“this field is
correct”), so the mean is a defensible, assumption-light pooling rule.

```pycon
>>> mean_probability({"judge": 0.9, "logprob": 0.7})
0.8
```

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

#### factory

alias of [`PlattCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.PlattCalibrator)

#### fit(signals, correct)

Fit one calibrator per signal name, then the `fusion` calibrator.

Each family is fit over the rows where it appears with a finite value. A
family with fewer than two such rows, or only one label class, cannot be
calibrated and is refused (`ValueError`) rather than turned into a
constant that would then dilute the fusion.

* **Return type:**
  [`SignalFamilyCalibrator`](_autosummary/ek.qe.calibrate.html.md#ek.qe.calibrate.SignalFamilyCalibrator)

#### fuse(calibrated)

Fuse per-family calibrated probabilities: `combine`, then `fusion`.

A single family’s value is returned as is: it is already calibrated, and
`fusion` was learned on fused values.

* **Return type:**
  [`float`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)

#### to_dict()

Serialize every family’s calibrator and the (registered) combiner’s name.

* **Return type:**
  [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)

### ek.qe.calibrate.expected_calibration_error(probs, correct, , n_bins=10)

Expected Calibration Error: weighted mean gap between confidence and accuracy.

# _autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md

# ek.qe.decide

Selective prediction: turn a calibrated probability into accept / flag / block.

Calibration makes a score *mean* something; a **decision policy** turns it into an
action with a guarantee (`misc/docs/ek_03` §3-4). This is the formal home of
“accept / flag / block” – a selective predictor that abstains (routes to a human)
rather than emit a low-confidence answer. Every policy here reads \*\*only calibrated
probabilities\*\* (Hard Rule 1): a raw score must already have passed through a
[`Calibrator`](_autosummary/ek.base.html.md#ek.base.Calibrator).

Three policies, by what you want to guarantee:

- [`CostSensitiveGate`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.CostSensitiveGate) – **the default**. The accept threshold falls out of the
  cost ratio `rho = c_FN / c_FP` on the calibrated probability; no labelled set
  needed once you know your costs.
- [`ConformalGate`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.ConformalGate) – split (inductive) conformal: a finite-sample,
  distribution-free **marginal** guarantee that at most `alpha` of truly-correct
  items are flagged. Per-field-type validity needs the Mondrian
  ([`GroupConformalGate`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.GroupConformalGate)) variant – conditional coverage is otherwise
  impossible (Barber et al. 2019).
- [`RiskControlGate`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.RiskControlGate) – conformal risk control: bound a monotone loss (the rate
  of accepted-yet-wrong items) at a target level.

[`risk_coverage_curve()`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.risk_coverage_curve) exposes the trade-off so stakeholders pick the operating
point explicitly. The pure-Python gates need no extra dependencies; the
`ek[calibration]` extra (MAPIE/crepes) offers library-backed conformal for an
sklearn-centric stack. Exchangeability is the load-bearing assumption – track
realised coverage and re-fit on drift.

### Example

```pycon
>>> from ek.base import Decision
>>> gate = CostSensitiveGate(rho=9.0)          # a false-negative costs 9x a review
>>> gate(0.95) is Decision.ACCEPT              # tau = rho/(1+rho) = 9/10 = 0.9
True
>>> gate(0.5) is Decision.FLAG
True
```

### Module Attributes

| [`DEFAULT_ALPHA`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.DEFAULT_ALPHA)       | Default target miscoverage for conformal gates (flag at most ~alpha of correct items).                                 |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [`DEFAULT_RISK_TARGET`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.DEFAULT_RISK_TARGET) | Default risk bound for [`RiskControlGate`](_autosummary/ek.qe.decide.html.md#ek.qe.decide.RiskControlGate) (accepted-error rate ceiling). |
